etymology: From Saxon etan, to eat, cognate with Latin edo and Greek edō. Hebrew 'akal is used of men, of beasts, of fire consuming, and of the sword devouring — the one verb covering nourishment and destruction, since to eat a thing is to make an end of it and to make it part of oneself.
biblical_def: The history of the race turns twice on a meal. The first fall is described in the plainest possible verbs: “the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes... she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat” (Genesis 3:6) — the whole ruin of Adam's posterity carried on an act of eating against a word of God. The recovery is announced in the same register, and it scandalised the crowd: “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you” (John 6:53). What the Lord requires there is not a physical mastication but a real receiving of Himself — faith doing with Christ what teeth do with bread, taking Him wholly in until He becomes the life of the man. Between the fall and the feast the ordinary meal remains a moral act. The passover was eaten standing and ready to march: “thus shall ye eat it; with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand” (Exodus 12:11). And Paul makes work the condition of bread in an ordered church: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Nothing in Scripture treats eating as a neutral animal function. It is obedience or rebellion, communion or gluttony, and the table is where a man's religion becomes visible.
webster_summary: To take food into the stomach; to consume; to devour. In Scripture, Eve took of the fruit and did eat; the passover eaten in haste with loins girded; Christ's command to eat His flesh and drink His blood; and the rule that he who will not work shall not eat.
webster_full: EAT, v.t. 1. To bite or chew and swallow, as food; to masticate and swallow for nourishment.
2. To corrode; to wear away; to consume, as fire or rust.
3. To enjoy; to partake of; as, to eat bread with a man, denoting fellowship.
4. From Saxon etan; Latin edo; Greek edo. The primary sense is to take in, to consume.
5. In Scripture, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, Gen. 3; except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, John 6.
corruption_summary: John 6 is pressed into a doctrine of physical eating, so that the Supper is made to convey Christ by digestion rather than by faith; and at the other pole, the table is stripped of moral weight altogether and eating treated as a matter beneath religion.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome takes the eating of John 6:53 as literal mastication and finds transubstantiation in it: the substance of the bread becomes the body of Christ, which is then eaten by the mouth, so that grace is conveyed by the act performed. Lutheran sacramental union softens the mechanism but keeps the oral eating. The Lord Himself forecloses the reading in the same discourse: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life” (John 6:63), and He identifies the eating with coming and believing in verse 35. The Reformed confession keeps everything the text says and refuses what it does not: Christ is truly received in the Supper, spiritually and really, by faith, so that the believer feeds on Him — while the unbeliever chews bread and receives judgment.

The opposite corruption is the modern indifference that treats appetite as an amoral appetite. Scripture does not agree. It names gluttony among the sins, sets a table before the believer as the highest picture of communion with God, makes the Supper the church's central act, and closes the canon with a marriage supper. Paul's rule — whether ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God — refuses the division of life into sacred acts and neutral ones. The principle to recover is that a man who cannot govern his eating has not yet learned that his body is not his own; and a church that eats together without discerning the Lord's body eats to its own harm.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'akal, to eat, consume, devour; lecheem, bread or food, that which is eaten; Greek esthiō, to eat, and trōgō, to chew or gnaw, used in John 6.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'akal (H398) — to eat, devour, consume; used alike of men at table, fire on a sacrifice, and the sword in battle.
Hebrew 'okel (H400) — food, that which is eaten; the noun of Genesis 3:6, the tree good for food.
Greek esthiō (G2068) — to eat; the ordinary verb, used of the passover and of the Lord's Supper.
Greek trōgō (G5176) — to gnaw or chew audibly; the deliberately physical verb of John 6:54-58, pressing the reality of the receiving.
Greek koinōnia (G2842) — communion, fellowship; the word Paul uses of the cup and the bread in 1 Corinthians 10:16.
usage: Of the first transgression: she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat (Genesis 3:6).
Of receiving Christ by faith: Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man... ye have no life in you (John 6:53).
Of ordered diligence in the church: if any would not work, neither should he eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

etymology: From Saxon drincan. Hebrew shathah is the plain verb to drink; mashqeh, the thing given to drink, is also the title of the king's cupbearer. In Scripture the noun often stands for the whole of what a man lives on, so that meat and drink together mean sustenance, and a drink offering means a life poured out.
biblical_def: Thirst is the condition Scripture assumes in every man, and the gospel is issued as an invitation to drink without money: “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat” (Isaiah 55:1). The Lord Jesus makes Himself the water and promises a permanence no cistern gives: “whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst” (John 4:14). Paul reads the wilderness history the same way — the rock struck in Horeb was not merely a providence but a type: “they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). And at the table the Lord takes the cup and sets a fixed term to His abstinence and a certain date to the church's hope: “I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom” (Matthew 26:29). Drinking therefore carries the whole doctrine of dependence. A man may go weeks without bread and days without water; the body was made to require what it cannot manufacture, and the soul was made the same way. To drink is to confess that life comes from outside oneself, which is the one confession the natural heart will not make until grace makes it thirsty.
webster_summary: To swallow liquid; to take in and be refreshed; also that which is drunk. In Scripture, the invitation to every one that thirsteth, the water Christ gives that a man may never thirst, the spiritual drink of the Rock in the wilderness, and the cup the Lord will drink new in His Father's kingdom.
webster_full: DRINK, v.t. 1. To swallow liquors; to quench thirst by swallowing water or other liquid.
2. To take in; to absorb; as, the earth drinks in the rain.
3. To partake of, as of a cup of suffering; as, to drink the cup appointed.
4. From Saxon drincan; the primary sense is to draw in.
5. In Scripture, whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst, John 4; they drank of that spiritual Rock, 1 Cor. 10.
corruption_summary: The cup is either forbidden absolutely, as though wine were sin in itself, or emptied of restraint altogether; and the Supper's cup is turned into a bare symbol on one side and a repeated sacrifice on the other.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors flank the biblical position on strong drink. Total abstinence pressed as a law of God adds to Scripture: the LORD gave wine to make glad the heart of man (Psalm 104:15), our Lord made it at Cana and drank it at table, and Paul prescribed a little of it for Timothy's infirmities. To call sin what God has blessed is the very error Paul names in 1 Timothy 4:3 as a doctrine of devils, and it has repeatedly bred hypocrisy where it has been imposed. The opposite licence is far more common and far more destructive: Scripture is unsparing about drunkenness, which it lists among the works of the flesh that bar men from the kingdom, and Proverbs 23 gives the drunkard's portrait with a realism no temperance tract improved on. Liberty of conscience governs the use; the plain prohibition governs the excess; and love of a weaker brother may require a man to forgo what he is free to take.

At the Lord's table a second corruption divides the church. The Roman Mass makes the cup the repeated offering of a sacrifice, which the epistle to the Hebrews forecloses by insisting that the offering was made once for all; bare memorialism, in reaction, empties the cup of everything but recollection, so that nothing is received. The Reformed confession holds the middle ground the text requires: the cup is the communion of the blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16), and the believer, by faith and by the working of the Holy Ghost, truly feeds on Christ crucified — not by the elements changing, but by the Spirit joining the believer to a Saviour who is in heaven. The Lord's own word at the institution fixes the direction to look: forward, to the day He drinks it new in His Father's kingdom.
roots_summary: Hebrew shathah, to drink; mashqeh, drink or cupbearer; Greek pinō, to drink, and potērion, the cup.
roots_lines: Hebrew shathah (H8354) — to drink; used of men, of beasts, and figuratively of drinking iniquity like water (Job 15:16).
Hebrew mashqeh (H4945) — drink, or the officer who gave it; Pharaoh's chief butler in Genesis 40.
Hebrew nesek (H5262) — a drink offering, poured out beside the sacrifice; the figure Paul takes for his own death (Philippians 2:17).
Greek pinō (G4095) — to drink; the verb of John 4:14 and of the institution of the Supper.
Greek potērion (G4221) — a cup; both the cup of blessing and the cup of God's wrath (Revelation 14:10).
usage: Of the free gospel offer: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters (Isaiah 55:1).
Of the water that satisfies for ever: whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst (John 4:14).
Of the wilderness type fulfilled: they drank of that spiritual Rock... and that Rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4).

etymology: From Old French taster, to handle or try, from Latin taxare, to touch or test — the original sense is to try a thing by handling, then by the tongue. Hebrew ta'am means both to taste and to perceive or discern, and the same noun means good judgment; the Hebrew treats discernment as a palate.
biblical_def: Scripture uses taste for the most personal kind of knowledge — not what a man has heard about a thing, but what he has had in his own mouth. The Psalmist's invitation is exactly that: “O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him” (Psalm 34:8). Peter takes the same verse into the new covenant as the ground of an appetite for the word: “If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious” (1 Peter 2:3). The word is then used for the deepest of all experiences, undergone in the sinner's room by the Son of God: “that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man” (Hebrews 2:9) — not a sip but the cup drained, since to taste death in the Hebrew idiom is to experience it fully. And the same epistle uses the word for a real but not saving acquaintance with divine things: men who “have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost” (Hebrews 6:4) and afterwards fall away. Taste therefore cuts two ways. It is the language of assurance, since a man who has tasted needs no argument that honey is sweet; and it is the language of solemn warning, since a man may taste much and never swallow.
webster_summary: To try or perceive by the tongue; to experience for oneself; also discernment or relish. In Scripture, taste and see that the LORD is good; having tasted that the Lord is gracious; Christ tasting death for every man; and those who taste of the heavenly gift and fall away.
webster_full: TASTE, v.t. 1. To perceive by means of the tongue; to have a sensation excited by something on the tongue.
2. To try by eating a little; to try the relish of.
3. To experience; to feel; to undergo; as, to taste of death.
4. From Old French taster, Latin taxare, to touch, to handle, to try.
5. In Scripture, O taste and see that the LORD is good, Ps. 34; taste death for every man, Heb. 2.
corruption_summary: Religious experience is made self-authenticating, so that having tasted something is taken as proof of conversion; and in reaction, others deny that Christianity is experienced at all and reduce it to assent.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 6:4 stands as a permanent rebuke to the assumption that a strong religious experience proves a saved man. The people described there were enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, were made partakers of the Holy Ghost in His common operations, tasted the good word of God and the powers of the world to come — and fell away. Much modern evangelism has no category for them, and so counts every emotional response as a new birth, records the decision, and leaves the man assured of a salvation he never received. The Reformed doctrine of perseverance answers this exactly: those who are truly regenerate persevere, and therefore falling away finally proves that the taste was never eating. “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The pastoral use of the text is not to unsettle the weak believer but to press every professor to examine whether he has trusted, not merely tasted.

The opposite error strips the Christian life of experience altogether, making faith a bare assent to propositions with no answering affection. Scripture will not have it. Psalm 34:8 commands a taste; Peter grounds a craving for the sincere milk of the word on having tasted grace; the Psalms are full of a delight that is felt. The Puritans were exact here and worth recovering: they distinguished between the affections wrought by the Spirit in a renewed heart and the transient impressions that common grace can raise in an unrenewed one, and they tested both by fruit and continuance rather than by intensity. Real tasting produces appetite, and appetite produces feeding, and feeding produces growth — and where those do not follow, the taste was a visit, not a home.
roots_summary: Hebrew ta'am, to taste and to perceive, with the noun meaning both flavour and discretion; Greek geuomai, to taste, and by idiom to experience.
roots_lines: Hebrew ta'am (H2938) — to taste, and thence to perceive or discern; “the mouth tasteth meat” (Job 34:3).
Hebrew ta'am (H2940) — taste, flavour, and also judgment or discretion; the manna tasted as wafers made with honey (Exodus 16:31).
Greek geuomai (G1089) — to taste, to eat, and idiomatically to experience fully; used of tasting death (Hebrews 2:9).
Greek chrēstos (G5543) — gracious, kind; the adjective Peter joins to tasting in 1 Peter 2:3.
Greek metochos (G3353) — a partaker or sharer; used of those made partakers of the Holy Ghost in Hebrews 6:4.
usage: Of experimental knowledge of God: O taste and see that the LORD is good (Psalm 34:8).
Of Christ's undergoing of death: that he by the grace of God should taste death for every man (Hebrews 2:9).
Of a real but unsaving acquaintance: have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost (Hebrews 6:4).

etymology: From French saveur, Latin sapor, taste or flavour, from sapere, to taste and also to be wise — the Latin joins discernment and flavour in one verb. In the Authorized Version savour usually renders the Hebrew rēach, a smell, especially the smell of a sacrifice ascending, and Greek osmē, an odour.
biblical_def: A savour in Scripture is chiefly a smell that rises, and it is the standing figure for a sacrifice God accepts. After the flood, the first recorded worship of the new world is met this way: “And the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake” (Genesis 8:21) — not that God has nostrils, but that the offering pleased Him and secured a promise. The New Testament identifies what all those altars were pointing at: “Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour” (Ephesians 5:2). The figure then extends to the church's witness, and with a terrible double edge: “we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish” (2 Corinthians 2:15) — the same gospel, the same preachers, and two opposite outcomes, so that faithfulness cannot be measured by reception. And the word is used of a quality that can be lost: “if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?” (Matthew 5:13). Savour is thus what a thing gives off — the sacrifice its smoke, the Christian his life, the salt its bite — and Scripture is concerned throughout with whether it rises to God or has gone flat.
webster_summary: Taste or odour; that which a thing gives off; in Scripture, the sweet savour of a sacrifice ascending to God, Christ's offering of Himself as a sweetsmelling savour, believers as a savour of Christ to the saved and the perishing, and salt that has lost its savour.
webster_full: SAVOUR, n. 1. Taste or odour; something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste or smell.
2. Scent; odour; as, a sweet savour.
3. Character or quality perceived; as, doctrine that has a savour of truth.
4. From French saveur, Latin sapor, from sapere, to taste, also to be wise.
5. In Scripture, the LORD smelled a sweet savour, Gen. 8; a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour, Eph. 5.
corruption_summary: The sweet savour is read as though God were appeased by the ritual itself, or else the whole sacrificial vocabulary is dismissed as primitive; and ministry is judged by how agreeable its savour proves to those who receive it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite misreadings of the sweet savour persist. The first is the pagan one Israel kept falling into, in which the smoke itself placates the deity, so that sacrifice becomes a transaction and the worshipper's heart is irrelevant. The prophets demolish this without qualification: God will not eat the flesh of bulls, He delights not in the blood of goats, and the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. The second is the modern dismissal, which reads the whole altar system as a primitive stage the faith outgrew, and then finds the doctrine of the atonement embarrassing for the same reason. But Ephesians 5:2 will not let the sacrificial category go: the death of Christ is presented as an offering and a sacrifice to God, offered by Him, received by the Father, and pleasing to Him. Take away the altar and the cross becomes an accident or a demonstration rather than a propitiation.

The second corruption is nearer to home. 2 Corinthians 2:15-16 says that faithful ministry smells of life to some and of death to others, and that the difference lies in the hearers, not in the savour. Modern ministry is routinely evaluated by the opposite rule: the measure of a message is how it lands, and a savour that offends is taken as proof that something went wrong. Paul says the reverse can be true, and asks “who is sufficient for these things?” The principle to recover is that the church's business is to be a sweet savour of Christ — faithful in doctrine and holy in life — and to leave the two outcomes with God. Salt that has lost its savour is not salt that has offended nobody; it is salt that has become indistinguishable from the meat it was meant to preserve.
roots_summary: Hebrew rēach, a smell or odour, especially of sacrifice; nīchoach, soothing or restful, the sweet savour of acceptance; Greek osmē, odour, and euodia, a fragrance.
roots_lines: Hebrew rēach (H7381) — a smell or odour; the standing word for the savour of an offering ascending.
Hebrew nīchoach (H5207) — soothing, restful; joined to rēach to mean a savour of rest or acceptance (Leviticus 1:9).
Greek osmē (G3744) — an odour or smell; used of the ointment that filled the house (John 12:3) and of the savour of Christ.
Greek euodia (G2175) — a sweet smell, fragrance; “a sweetsmelling savour” (Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 4:18).
Greek mōrainō (G3471) — to make foolish or insipid; the verb behind salt that has lost its savour (Matthew 5:13).
usage: Of a sacrifice accepted: the LORD smelled a sweet savour (Genesis 8:21).
Of the atonement offered to God: a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour (Ephesians 5:2).
Of ministry with two outcomes: a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish (2 Corinthians 2:15).

etymology: From Saxon cruma, a small fragment of bread. In the Gospels the word is the diminutive psichion, a little morsel — the scraps that fall from a table during a meal, which in an eastern house went to the dogs beneath it.
biblical_def: The crumb appears in Scripture at exactly two tables, and both are about who has a right to be fed. The first is in Tyre and Sidon, where a Gentile woman meets a hard word from the Lord and does not argue with it: “Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table” (Matthew 15:27); Mark records her answer in the same terms (Mark 7:28). She concedes the whole of Israel's covenant priority, asks for nothing that would displace the children, and requests only what falls — and the Lord calls it great faith and heals her daughter. The second table is Dives' own, and the crumb condemns rather than saves: Lazarus lay at the gate, “desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table” (Luke 16:21) — and did not get them. Against both stands the Lord's own economy after the feeding of the multitude: “Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost” (John 6:12). The crumb is therefore a measure of two things at once: of a faith so lowly it will take the least of Christ rather than none of Him, and of a hardness so complete that it will not part with what it was throwing away.
webster_summary: A small fragment or piece of bread; a little morsel that falls from the table. In Scripture, the crumbs the Canaanite woman asked for and received, the crumbs Lazarus desired and was denied, and the fragments Christ commanded to be gathered that nothing be lost.
webster_full: CRUMB, n. 1. A fragment or small piece of bread broken or cut off.
2. The soft part of bread, as distinguished from the crust.
3. A small particle of anything; a little portion.
4. From Saxon cruma, a fragment; the primary sense is that which is rubbed or broken off.
5. In Scripture, the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table, Matt. 15.
corruption_summary: The Canaanite woman's exchange is read as a rebuke of Christ for prejudice which she corrects, inverting the account; and the crumb is preached as an emblem of a stingy God who gives His people scraps.
corruption_paragraphs: A now-common reading of Matthew 15 has the woman educating Jesus out of an ethnic narrowness He had absorbed from His culture, so that the story becomes a lesson in the expansion of a limited mind. That reading is impossible on any orthodox Christology: He who is very God of very God, without sin, did not need instruction in mercy from a Canaanite. Nor does the text support it. The Lord states the redemptive-historical order — He was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, the children fed first — which is the same order Paul states in Romans 1:16, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. He tests her, as He tested Jacob at the ford and the disciples in the storm, and He praises the faith the test produced. She does not overturn His words; she believes them and finds mercy inside them, which is why He answers, “O woman, great is thy faith.”

The second corruption sentimentalises the crumb in the other direction, as though God's people were left picking scraps under the table while the real feast belonged elsewhere. The parable of Lazarus corrects that with its ending, not its beginning: the man who could not get a crumb was carried by angels into Abraham's bosom, and the man with the full table lifted up his eyes in torment. And the Lord who spoke of crumbs also fed five thousand until they were filled and had twelve baskets over. The principle to recover is the posture the woman took — asking for nothing on the ground of desert, and finding that grace in the hand of Christ is never rationed to those who come that way.
roots_summary: Greek psichion, a little crumb or morsel, diminutive of psix, a bit; the fragments of John 6 are klasmata, broken pieces.
roots_lines: Greek psichion (G5589) — a crumb or small morsel; used only of the crumbs beneath the table (Matthew 15:27; Mark 7:28; Luke 16:21).
Greek klasma (G2801) — a broken piece or fragment; the twelve baskets gathered after the feeding (John 6:12-13).
Greek kynarion (G2952) — a little dog, a household dog; the diminutive softens the term and the woman seizes on it.
Greek trapeza (G5132) — a table; both the household table of the parable and the Lord's table (1 Corinthians 10:21).
Hebrew path (H6595) — a morsel or bit of bread; “a morsel of bread” brought to the three visitors (Genesis 18:5).
usage: Of great faith content with the least of Christ: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table (Matthew 15:27).
Of hardness at a full table: desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table (Luke 16:21).
Of Christ's care that nothing be wasted: Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost (John 6:12).

Mark 7:28

etymology: From Saxon braeth, breath, vapour, exhalation. Hebrew has two words the English merges: neshamah, the breath of life God breathed into man's nostrils, and ruach, wind, breath, or spirit. Greek pnoē is a blowing or breath, from pneō, to blow, the root of pneuma.
biblical_def: Breath in Scripture is the borrowed thing on which every living creature depends moment by moment. Elihu states both the origin and the ownership: “The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life” (Job 33:4). Paul preaches the same doctrine to philosophers on Mars' hill, and draws from it the uselessness of temples built to supply God's needs: “he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things” (Acts 17:25). Because breath is a gift and not a possession, the mere fact of having it constitutes an obligation, and the Psalter ends on exactly that note: “Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD” (Psalm 150:6) — the last verse of the book, and the widest command in it. And breath is what God supplies when He raises the dead: in the valley of dry bones the sinews and flesh come first and the corpses still do not live until He says, “Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live” (Ezekiel 37:5). That order is the doctrine of regeneration in a vision. A man may be assembled, instructed, and outwardly complete, and remain a corpse until God breathes; and when He does, the life is undeniably His and not the bones'.
webster_summary: The air drawn into and expelled from the lungs; the life that depends on it. In Scripture, the breath of the Almighty that gives life, God giving to all life and breath, everything that hath breath commanded to praise the LORD, and the breath He causes to enter dry bones that they may live.
webster_full: BREATH, n. 1. The air inhaled and expelled in the respiration of animals.
2. Life; the power of respiring, and hence, existence itself.
3. A single respiration; hence a moment, an instant; also a gentle breeze.
4. From Saxon braeth, an exhalation, vapour, breath.
5. In Scripture, the breath of the Almighty hath given me life, Job 33; let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD, Ps. 150.
corruption_summary: Life is treated as a property the creature owns, so that its beginning and end become matters of human choice; and the divine breath is reduced to a metaphor for an impersonal life-force shared by all things.
corruption_paragraphs: If breath is given moment by moment by God, then life is held on loan and no man is proprietor of his own or another's. That single premise stands against the age at both ends of life. The unborn child, whose members were written in God's book before they were formed, is not disposable tissue; the aged and the suffering, whose breath God still gives, are not candidates for a managed exit dressed up as dignity. Daniel put it to Belshazzar without softening: “the God in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all thy ways, hast thou not glorified” (Daniel 5:23). Every argument for autonomy over life begins by denying that clause, and the denial is not usually stated — it is assumed, and then the ethics follow easily.

The second corruption runs the other way, dissolving the personal Giver into an impersonal energy. Panentheist and process theologies make the divine breath the animating principle immanent in all things, so that God is the life of the world rather than its Creator, and the difference between Him and His creatures is one of degree. Scripture keeps the distinction absolute: God gives breath, and He is not Himself the breath He gives; He is aseity itself, needing nothing, worshipped not with men's hands as though He needed any thing. The practical difference is the whole of religion. An impersonal life-force cannot be praised, cannot be sinned against, and cannot raise the dead — and the LORD who breathed into Adam's nostrils, and who breathes upon dry bones, does all three.
roots_summary: Hebrew neshamah, the breath of life breathed into man; ruach, breath, wind, or spirit; Greek pnoē, a breath or blowing, and pneuma, spirit.
roots_lines: Hebrew neshamah (H5397) — breath, especially the breath of life God breathed into Adam (Genesis 2:7); also the spirit of man as the candle of the LORD (Proverbs 20:27).
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — wind, breath, spirit; the word of Ezekiel 37, where wind, breath, and Spirit are the same term.
Greek pnoē (G4157) — breath, a blowing; used of God giving breath (Acts 17:25) and of the rushing mighty wind at Pentecost (Acts 2:2).
Greek pneuma (G4151) — spirit, breath, wind; the Holy Ghost, and the human spirit rendered up at death.
Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed; the adjective describing Scripture in 2 Timothy 3:16.

Of the universal obligation to praise: Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD (Psalm 150:6).
Of resurrection and regeneration: I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live (Ezekiel 37:5).

etymology: From Saxon baelg, a bag or skin, whence also bellows — the belly is the body's bag. Hebrew beten is the abdomen or womb; me'eh, the inward parts. Greek koilia is a hollow, used of the stomach, the womb, and figuratively of the innermost man.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses belly where modern speech would say stomach, womb, or the inward man, and Scripture puts it to work in three directions. It is the seat of appetite, and appetite can be enthroned: Paul writes of men “whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things” (Philippians 3:19) — a religion of gratification, and he weeps as he names it. It is the place of confinement in the great sign of the resurrection: “as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40), and Jonah himself prays from a deeper place still: “out of the belly of hell cried I” (Jonah 2:2). And it is the innermost man from which the Spirit's supply overflows to others: “He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38). Set together, these uses are a small anatomy of the heart. The same interior can be a god demanding to be fed, a grave from which a man cries, or a spring from which rivers run; and which it is depends on whether the Holy Ghost has taken possession of it.
webster_summary: The part of the body containing the bowels; the womb; and by figure the innermost part of a man. In Scripture, those whose God is their belly, Jonah in the whale's belly and crying from the belly of hell, and the believer out of whose belly flow rivers of living water.
webster_full: BELLY, n. 1. That part of the human body which extends from the breast to the thighs, containing the bowels.
2. The womb. Jer. 1.
3. The part of anything which resembles the human belly in protuberance or cavity; as, the belly of a flagon.
4. From Saxon baelg, a bag or skin; whence bellows, a bag for wind.
5. In Scripture, whose God is their belly, Phil. 3; out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water, John 7.
corruption_summary: Bodily appetite is treated as morally neutral and therefore ungovernable, so that self-indulgence loses the name of idolatry; and the body itself is either despised as the soul's prison or exalted as the whole of the man.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul does not call the men of Philippians 3:19 weak; he calls their belly their god, which makes indulgence a form of worship and not merely a failure of willpower. That category has almost disappeared. Appetite — for food, for drink, for sexual gratification, for comfort, for the endless small consumptions the age arranges to be always available — is now discussed as preference, or as wiring, or at worst as an unhealthy pattern to be managed. Scripture's word is idolatry, and the remedy is correspondingly larger: not technique but repentance, not management but a rival love. The apostle's own answer in the same passage is to set the citizenship in heaven and the coming of the Saviour against the earthly mind, because an appetite is only dethroned by a better object.

The two errors about the body itself flank this. Ancient gnosticism, and the ascetic strain that survived it, treated the flesh as the soul's prison and holiness as escape from it, which Colossians 2:23 answers directly: such severity to the body is of no value against the indulgence of the flesh. The modern error is the opposite, treating the body as the whole of a man and its satisfactions as the sum of his good. Scripture holds the true doctrine between them: the body is the temple of the Holy Ghost, bought with a price, destined for resurrection, and therefore neither to be despised nor obeyed. John 7:38 gives the positive picture — an inward man so filled by the Spirit that what comes out of him is a river for others, which is exactly what a belly-god can never produce.
roots_summary: Hebrew beten, the belly or womb; me'eh, the inward parts or bowels; Greek koilia, a hollow, the stomach, the womb, and the inner man.
roots_lines: Hebrew beten (H990) — the belly, and frequently the womb; “before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee” (Jeremiah 1:5).
Hebrew me'eh (H4578) — the inward parts, bowels; the seat of deep feeling in Hebrew idiom (Isaiah 16:11).
Hebrew mē'āh in Jonah 2:1 — the fish's inward parts, from which the prophet's psalm is prayed.
Greek koilia (G2836) — a hollow; the belly, the womb, and by figure the innermost being (John 7:38).
Greek gastēr (G1064) — the stomach or womb; whence gastrimargia, gluttony, in later Greek moral writing.
usage: Of appetite enthroned as a god: whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame (Philippians 3:19).
Of the sign of the prophet Jonas: as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly (Matthew 12:40).
Of the Spirit's overflow in a believer: out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water (John 7:38).

etymology: From Old French feindre, to feign or shrink back, hence to give way, to lose heart. The Hebrew words describe both bodily exhaustion and the collapse of courage, and the Greek ekluō means literally to be loosed out — the strings of a man slackened until he can no longer hold together.
biblical_def: To faint in Scripture is to run out — of strength, of courage, or of endurance — and God's dealings with fainting men are among the tenderest passages in the Bible. Isaiah sets the promise against the plain fact of human limit: “He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength” (Isaiah 40:29), and then the great promise that follows: “they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). Note the descending order — mounting, running, walking — ending not with ecstasy but with the ordinary plod that outlasts everything. Paul applies the same word to the long obedience of well-doing: “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Galatians 6:9). And the Lord Jesus gives fainting as the alternative to praying: He “spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luke 18:1). That verse fixes the doctrine. There are only two responses to a burden that exceeds a man's strength: he prays, or he faints. Prayer is not a technique for the strong but the appointed refuge of those who have already discovered they cannot.
webster_summary: To lose strength or courage; to sink into dejection or swoon; also weak, languid, dim. In Scripture, God giving power to the faint, those who wait on the LORD walking and not fainting, the command not to be weary in well doing, and the parable teaching men to pray and not to faint.
webster_full: FAINT, a. 1. Weak; languid; inclined to swoon; destitute of strength.
2. Wanting courage or spirit; dejected; depressed; timorous.
3. Not bright or vivid; dim; as, a faint colour, a faint light.
4. From Old French feindre, to shrink or give way; the primary sense is to yield or fail.
5. In Scripture, they shall walk, and not faint, Isa. 40; men ought always to pray, and not to faint, Luke 18.
corruption_summary: Weariness in the Christian life is reclassified as a wound to be treated rather than a weakness to be brought to God, so that the promised remedy of waiting on the LORD is replaced by rest technique, self-care, and the counsel to expect less of oneself.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapy-culture vocabulary has largely taken over the way churches speak about exhaustion. What Scripture calls fainting is now burnout, depletion, or an empty cup, and the prescriptions follow the diagnosis: boundaries, self-care, and a reduced expectation of duty. Some of that counsel is ordinary wisdom — the body has limits, Elijah under the juniper tree was fed and made to sleep before he was reasoned with, and God remembers that we are dust. But the biblical remedy is never merely the removal of demand. Isaiah's promise is renewal of strength in the running and the walking, given to those who wait upon the LORD, which is an activity of faith and not a suspension of it; and the Lord's answer to fainting is a parable about a widow who kept coming. Where the modern counsel stops at rest, Scripture sends the weary man to the throne of grace to find help in time of need.

The opposite error is to preach endurance as though it were self-generated, so that a fainting believer concludes he must try harder and is crushed by a standard no one can carry. Galatians 6:9 is not a demand for grit; it is a promise attached to a harvest — in due season we shall reap — and the season is God's to appoint. The principle to recover joins both halves: strength for the ordinary walk is real, is promised, and is God's gift, given not to the mighty but expressly to them that have no might. That is why perseverance is a doctrine of grace and not a virtue of the strong, and why the saints who last longest are usually those who learned earliest that they could not.
roots_summary: Hebrew ya'aph, to be weary or faint; 'alaph, to be overcome or swoon; Greek ekluō, to be loosed out or exhausted, and ekkakeō, to lose heart.
roots_lines: Hebrew ya'aph (H3286) — to be weary, to faint; used of the young men who shall utterly fall in Isaiah 40:30.
Hebrew 'alaph (H5968) — to cover, and thence to faint or swoon; Jonah fainted when the sun beat on his head (Jonah 4:8).
Hebrew qavah (H6960) — to wait, to look for with expectation; the verb behind “they that wait upon the LORD” (Isaiah 40:31).
Greek ekluō (G1590) — to loose out, to relax utterly, to faint; used of the multitude who would faint by the way (Matthew 15:32).
Greek ekkakeō (G1573) — to lose heart, to grow weary in doing; the verb of Galatians 6:9 and Luke 18:1.
usage: Of strength given to the exhausted: He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength (Isaiah 40:29).
Of perseverance in ordinary duty: in due season we shall reap, if we faint not (Galatians 6:9).
Of the alternative to prayer: men ought always to pray, and not to faint (Luke 18:1).

etymology: From Saxon hnecca. Hebrew has two words with opposite moral colour: tsavva'r, the neck that receives a yoke or an embrace, and 'oreph, the back of the neck — the part a man turns toward you when he refuses, whence the biblical adjective stiffnecked, from an ox that will not bow to the yoke.
biblical_def: The neck is where a man's submission or his refusal becomes visible, because it is the part that bows or stiffens. Scripture's standing charge against Israel is drawn from the plough: “He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy” (Proverbs 29:1) — the ox that will not take the yoke, and the man who will not take reproof, come to the same end. At the Jerusalem council Peter uses the figure against a false yoke, not a true one: “why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10) — the law as a way of justification is a burden no neck could carry, and to lay it on Gentile believers is to tempt God. But the neck is also where love lands. Joseph, at the end of twenty-two years of grief, “fell upon his brother Benjamin's neck, and wept” (Genesis 45:14); and the Lord Jesus puts the same gesture in the mouth of the Father Himself: while the prodigal was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck (Luke 15:20). Stiffened, it is the emblem of rebellion; bowed to Christ's easy yoke, it is the emblem of a servant; and wept upon, it is the emblem of a welcome no returning sinner deserves.
webster_summary: The part of the body between the head and trunk; in Scripture, the neck that bears a yoke, the hardened or stiff neck of the rebel, the unbearable yoke Peter refused to lay on the disciples, and the neck fallen upon in embrace by Joseph and by the father of the prodigal.
webster_full: NECK, n. 1. The part of an animal's body which is between the head and the trunk, and connects them.
2. A long narrow tract of land projecting from the main body; as, a neck of land.
3. In Scripture, a stiff neck denotes obstinacy in sin; to fall on the neck denotes affection and welcome.
4. From Saxon hnecca, the neck or nape.
5. In Scripture, he that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, Prov. 29; fell on his neck, and kissed him, Luke 15.
corruption_summary: Submission itself is treated as the injury, so that any yoke is called oppression and the stiff neck is renamed authenticity; while in the other direction, false yokes Scripture never imposed are laid on consciences in the name of obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has made an unbowed neck into a virtue. To submit — to God's word, to lawful authority in home, church, or state — is presented as the surrender of the self, and resistance as integrity. The biblical assessment is the reverse: the stiff neck is not strength but stubbornness under reproof, and Proverbs 29:1 attaches a terrible consequence to it, sudden destruction without remedy. What makes the modern form dangerous is that it is often sincere; the man believes he is being true to himself when in fact he is refusing correction he knows to be just. Scripture's alternative is not a broken man but a yoked one, and the Lord Jesus describes His own yoke as easy and His burden light — a yoke that does not crush the neck it fits but makes the work possible.

The opposite corruption is the one Peter confronted at Jerusalem: yokes God never laid. Circumcision and the ceremonial law were being pressed on Gentile believers as necessary to salvation, and Peter called it tempting God. The forms recur wherever human rules are given the force of divine command — a required diet, a required calendar, a required style, a required political allegiance — and made the test of a man's standing. The principle to recover cuts both ways at once: no man may refuse the yoke Christ lays, and no man may impose a yoke Christ has not. Between those two lies the liberty of conscience that Scripture alone binds, and the tenderness of a Father who runs to a neck he has every right to break.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsavva'r, the neck as bearing a yoke or receiving an embrace; 'oreph, the back of the neck, whence stiffnecked; Greek trachēlos, the neck.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsavva'r (H6677) — the neck; the part that bears the yoke (Jeremiah 27:8) and that Joseph fell upon (Genesis 45:14).
Hebrew 'oreph (H6203) — the back of the neck, the nape; joined to qashah, to harden, in the charge stiffnecked (Exodus 32:9).
Hebrew qashah (H7185) — to be hard, severe, obstinate; the verb of hardening the neck against reproof.

etymology: From Old French logne, Latin lumbus, the loin. The loins are the small of the back and the hips — in Scripture the seat of a man's strength for labour and travel, and by a common Hebrew figure the source of his descendants, who are said to come out of his loins.
biblical_def: Because the eastern robe was long and loose, a man about to work, run, or fight gathered it up and tucked it into his belt — he girded his loins — and Scripture makes that gesture a standing figure for readiness. The passover was eaten in exactly that posture: “thus shall ye eat it; with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand” (Exodus 12:11) — a redeemed people dressed to leave. The Lord Jesus commands the same posture toward His return: “Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning” (Luke 12:35). Peter moves the figure inward, where the real slackness lies: “gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:13) — a mind gathered up, not trailing loose in speculation and drift. And Paul puts the girdle first in the armour, because everything else hangs on it: “having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness” (Ephesians 6:14). The order is deliberate. Truth is not one weapon among the rest; it is the belt that holds the soldier together, and a man loose at that point will lose the use of every other piece.
webster_summary: The space on each side of the vertebrae between the ribs and the hips; the seat of strength, and by figure the source of offspring. In Scripture, the passover eaten with loins girded, loins girded about with truth, the loins of the mind girded up, and the command to have loins girded and lights burning.
webster_full: LOINS, n. plu. 1. The space on each side of the vertebrae, between the lowest of the false ribs and the upper portion of the hip bone.
2. The reins; regarded as the seat of strength and of generative power.
3. To gird the loins, to prepare for action, labour, or a journey, by binding up the flowing garment.
4. From Old French logne, Latin lumbus, the loin.
5. In Scripture, with your loins girded, Exod. 12; gird up the loins of your mind, 1 Pet. 1.
corruption_summary: Readiness for Christ's return is replaced by a settled expectation that history will simply continue, so that watchfulness becomes an embarrassment; and the girdle of truth is loosened by a faith that prizes sincerity above doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: The posture Christ commanded — loins girded, lights burning, men that wait for their lord — assumes He is coming and that the hour is unknown. Two habits have quietly displaced it. The first is the practical settledness of comfortable churches, which plan and build and invest as though history were a level road with no end, and for which the second coming is a doctrine affirmed on paper and never reckoned with. The second is the reaction to date-setting: because sensational prophecy charts have repeatedly failed and embarrassed the church, watchfulness itself is treated as the province of cranks. But Scripture does not offer a third option between speculation and complacency; it commands readiness, which is a moral posture rather than a chronological calculation. The servant is not told to know the hour. He is told to be dressed.

The girdle of truth loosens by a different mechanism. Where sincerity is prized above doctrine, a man may hold almost anything provided he holds it warmly, and the belt that gathers the whole armour is left hanging. Paul's order in Ephesians 6 is a rebuke to that: the breastplate, the shoes, the shield, the helmet, and the sword all presuppose a man already girt with truth, since a soldier whose robe is loose cannot use any of them. The principle to recover is that doctrine is not the enemy of readiness but its condition. A church that knows what it believes can wait, work, and suffer; a church that has loosened the belt trips over its own garments at the first alarm.
roots_summary: Hebrew mothnayim, the loins or hips; chalatsayim, the loins as the seat of strength and offspring; Greek osphys, the loin, both literal and figurative.
roots_lines: Hebrew mothnayim (H4975) — the loins; girded for service (Exodus 12:11) and loosed in terror (Daniel 5:6).
Hebrew chalatsayim (H2504) — the loins; used of descendants said to come out of a man's loins (Genesis 35:11).
Hebrew 'azar (H247) — to gird, to bind about; “Gird up now thy loins like a man” (Job 38:3).
Greek osphys (G3751) — the loin; the loins of the mind (1 Peter 1:13) and Levi in the loins of Abraham (Hebrews 7:10).
Greek perizonnymi (G4024) — to gird about; the verb of Luke 12:35 and Ephesians 6:14.

Of the mind gathered up for hope: gird up the loins of your mind, be sober (1 Peter 1:13).
